fieldReview.recordValue: Mechanic – Songs   Musician Songs can be triggered one of four ways. Regardless of the Area of Effect, Songs always affect the user. » When using a Move with the Sonic keyword, Songs may be triggered as a Rapid Action, and the Song’s Area of Effect is the same as the triggering Move’s. » When using a Dance Move, Songs may be triggered as a Shift Action with an Area of Effect of Burst 2. » As a Standard Action, you may trigger one Song, with an Area of Effect of Burst 4. » As a Full Action, you may trigger two Songs, each with an Area of Effect of Burst 4.

fieldReview.recordValue: Mechanic – Dance Moves: Dance Moves you create with the Dance Form Feature look like the Move on the right. First, name the Dance Move whatever you like. Secondly, choose two Combat Stage gains for the effect. This may either be +2 Combat Stages to a single Stat, like Swords Dance, or +1 Combat Stage to two different Stats, like Dragon Dance. Once chosen, this cannot be changed. Dragon Dance, Quiver Dance, and Swords Dance count as Dance Moves for the purposes of Dancer Features as well. A Dance Move’s Contest Type must be chosen from a Contest Type associated with a Stat that the Dance Move affects. Cool is associated with Attack, Tough is associated with Defense, Beauty is associated with Special Attack, Smart is associated with Special Defense, and Cute is associated with Speed.  Name Type: Normal Frequency: EOT AC: None Class: Status Range: Self Effect: Contest Type: Contest Effect: Get Ready!

fieldReview.recordValue:
Terastalization is a type of enhancement and transformation that affects a Pokémon, blinging it out in a massive jewel. Two prerequisites must be met before a Pokémon can Terastalize: the Trainer must be wearing an Accessory Slot Item called a Tera Orb, and the Tera Orb must have accumulated enough energy to initiate and sustain the phenomenon.

When a Pokémon Terastalizes, its Typing is completely overridden to its Tera Type. A Pokémon’s Tera Type is defined through a Capability denoting which Tera Type it has. The Tera Type for a Pokémon is usually its default Type (or one of its default Types) but through special means a Pokémon can have a different Tera Type or be given a new one. When generated or caught, a Pokémon has an 80% chance for its Tera Type to be one of its default Type(s), and 20% to be any other base Type, including the Stellar-Type. GMs including Types beyond the original 18 and Stellar (like Nuclear and Shadow) can choose to allow Pokémon to have Tera Types beyond the basic 19.

Trainers with Type Sync can change a Pokémon’s Tera Type to match the Type(s) they have access to through Type Sync. Otherwise, GMs are recommended to make “Type Shifters” available to change their players’ Pokémon’s Tera Types, akin to NPC Move Tutors. Consider having this service cost 5000₽.

While Terastilized, a Pokémon cannot have its Typing changed from its Tera Type. A Terastalized Pokémon still receives STAB for its original Types, and receives an extra STAB for its Tera Type (apply the in-system Type STAB Boost effects to the Pokémon). If the Tera Type is the same as one of the original Types, this STAB doubles up (so a move gets +4 DB). When a Pokémon Terastalizes into the Stellar-Type, it still receives STAB for its original Types. The Pokémon then gains a extra STAB bonus for every Type. Once the Pokémon uses a Move of a given Type, it loses that extra STAB for that Type for the remainder of their Terastilization.

Note: the Stellar-Type confers no resistances, but has no weaknesses and no Moves may be Tera Type. Logistically, a Stellar-Type Pokémon has no Type-based weaknesses, though certain Moves and Abilities may allow separate increases in effectiveness.

Terastalization can be triggered on either the Pokémon or the Trainer’s turn as a Standard Action. Once triggered, Terastalization lasts for the rest of the Scene, even if the Pokémon is knocked out. A Tera Orb can only fuel one Terastalization at a time, meaning once a Trainer Terastalizes a Pokémon, they can’t Terastalize until the Tera Orb is recharged.
Note: If a Trainer is incapacitated before the Terastalization activation completely resolves, the Tera Orb’s charge is not expended and the target isn’t Terastalized, but the Trainer still uses their Standard Action.

Note: The Terastal phenomenon is most unexplained in the video games, but is primarily tied to phenomena surrounding the Paldea Region’s Area Zero. Like with Dynamax, it is recommended for GMs to be particularly scrutinizing with how they manage the availability of Tera Orbs and their methods to allow Pokémon to alter their Tera Typing, as Terastalization has the potential for significant mechanical and narrative consequences.

fieldReview.recordValue:
Moves with this Keyword cannot Miss when rolling with an Accuracy Roll, meaning that effects that make Moves Miss can still make Max Moves Miss, and that Max Moves may trigger Critical Hits or Effect Ranges.

If a Max Move Misses, instead of doing no damage, they deal damage as if the attack was resisted two steps further. Targets dealt damage this way still suffer any secondary effects. This means Max Moves ignores effects that would prevent the damage or effects from applying to a target.

Max Moves may be either Physical or Special.

Max Moves may not be otherwise modified or given the “Friendly” Keyword.

fieldReview.recordValue:
Basic Cases
Prerequisites: Jailbreaker
Effect: You may create a Contest Case, Lock Case, or Medicine Case for $200.

Trick Cases
Prerequisites: Case Specialist
Effect: You may create a Spray Case, Flash Case, or Bounce Case for $400.

Advanced Cases
Prerequisites: Fusion Cases
Effect: You may create a Zap Case for $500, a Devil Case for $1000, or a Storage Case for $5000.

Poké Ball Modifications
Habitat Modification
Ingredients/Cost: Dive Ball / $250
Effect: Add one of the following keywords to the targeted Dive Ball: Arctic, Mountain, Desert, Grassland, Rainforest, Forest, Tundra, Taiga, Marsh, Beach, Freshwater, Urban or Cave. Instead of when underwater or underground, the modified Poké Ball subtracts 20 from its Capture Rolls when thrown in an area that corresponds with the keyword chosen.

Power Modification
Ingredients/Cost: Nest Ball / $500
Effect: You change the Nest Ball into a Power Ball. It retains the conditional capture modifier of a Nest Ball, but additionally, when a Power Ball captures a target, the captured Pokémon is raised 1d4 levels upon capture.

Type Modification
Ingredients/Cost: Net Ball / $300
Effect: You change the Net Ball into an Earth Ball, Haunt Ball, Solid Ball, Heat Ball, Mystic Ball, Air Ball, Mold Ball, or Gossamer Ball. The properties of these unique balls are identical to the Net Ball, but instead of affecting Bug and Water types, these Balls correspond to the following types. Earth Ball; Grass and Ground; Haunt Ball, Dark and Ghost; Solid Ball, Rock and Steel; Heat Ball, Electric and Fire; Mystic Ball, Dragon and Psychic; Air Ball, Flying and Ice; Mold Ball, Poison and Fighting; Gossamer Ball, Normal and Fairy.

Fabulous Modification
Ingredients/Cost: Luxury Ball / $250
Effect: You change the Luxury Ball into an Fabulous Ball. When a Fabulous Ball captures a target, the captured Pokémon gains +2 dice in the Contest Stat that corresponds to the Stat boosted by their Nature. If the Stat boosted is HP, choose any two Contest Stats except the one corresponding to the lowered Stat and raise them by 1 die each. As a reminder, Beauty=SpAtk, Cool=Attack, Cute=Speed, Smart=SpDef, Tough=Def.

Learning Modification
Ingredients/Cost: Friend Ball / $500
Effect: You change the Friend Ball into a Learning Ball. Instead of increasing loyalty upon capture, when a Learning Ball captures a target, the captured Pokémon immediately learns their next level-up Move, as long as it is within 8 levels of their current level.

Weather Modification
Ingredients/Cost: Dusk Ball / $300
Effect: You change the Dusk Ball into a Sun Ball, Rain Ball, Hail Ball, or Sand Ball. Instead of when in low light, the modified Poké Ball subtracts 20 from its Capture Rolls when thrown during the corresponding weather effect.

Note: Learning, Fabulous and Power Modification work once on a Pokémon.

fieldReview.recordValue: Mechanic: While Channeling a Pokémon, it may communicate its intentions, emotions, and motivations to you and you may communicate similarly with them; neither party may be deceitful in this exchange. You also become aware of all of its Moves, Abilities, and Capabilities. Allied Channeled Pokémon may always attempt Intercept Maneuvers for each other, regardless of Loyalty. If you are Fainted, you stop Channeling all Pokémon. Whenever you Channel a Pokémon, you have a vague knowledge of what has happened in the Pokémon’s past hour as if they were your own memories.  Note: Channeler has a couple Features with the [Orders] tag. However, because they require that a Pokémon be Channeled, which isn’t League Legal, they actually aren’t of any use in League Legal battles!

fields.recordValue: Mechanic: While Channeling a Pokémon, it may communicate its intentions, emotions, and motivations to you and you may communicate similarly with them; neither party may be deceitful in this exchange. You also become aware of all of its Moves, Abilities, and Capabilities. Allied Channeled Pokémon may always attempt Intercept Maneuvers for each other, regardless of Loyalty. If you are Fainted, you stop Channeling all Pokémon. Whenever you Channel a Pokémon, you have a vague knowledge of what has happened in the Pokémon’s past hour as if they were your own memories.  Note: Channeler has a couple Features with the [Orders] tag. However, because they require that a Pokémon be Channeled, which isn’t League Legal, they actually aren’t of any use in League Legal battles!

Messiah Effect: You become aware of any Pacts, Patrons, or Allegiances the Target may have to a Legendary being or any organizations. If this Target has a particular weakness (Both Narrative and mechanical), you become aware of it. You also become aware of any goals or motives the Target might possess at the moment. If this target aligned to a Legendary or an organization, you become of aware of this fact, but not of who or what in particular. You also learn if this Targets motives or goals would harm your Patron or their followers.

fieldReview.recordValue:
A Zenith Move (shortened to Z-Move) is a special type of Move, in which a Trainer and their Pokémon's wishes combine to unleash an attack comprising the full power of both. The Trainer focuses their will into a stone known as a Zenith Core, which magnifies and transmits that innate power between a pair of Z-Crystals that both the Trainer and Pokémon hold, allowing the Pokemon to transform one of its Moves into a powerful Z-Move.

When a Pokémon attempts to use a Damaging Move with a Type corresponding to a Z-Crystal held by the Pokémon and the Trainer, the Trainer can transform that Move into a Z-Move as a Full Action Reaction. These Z-Moves are very powerful, but a Zenith Core can only fuel a single Z-Move per Scene. If an Interrupt is used so that the target is instead not hit by the move, the target instead takes damage as if 2 steps more resistant to the attack (just as Smite causes 1 more step of resistance for misses, these don’t stack, so using Protect against a miss is still only 2 steps more resistant on top of type matchups)

Note: If a Trainer is incapacitated before the Z-Move activation completely resolves, the Zenith Core’s charge is not expended and the Z-Move isn’t used, but the Trainer still uses their Full Action.

There are 18 different Z-Crystals that correspond to each of the 18 types, with several others that correspond to specific Pokémon. When a Trainer obtains a Z-Crystal that they can hold, they may then craft Z-Crystals that their Pokemon may hold. By default, a Trainer may only have the Zenith Core and one variety of Z-Crystal equipped at one time.

It is recommended for GMs to give a few Z-Crystals out to their players as valuable rewards for quests, prizes for winning tournaments, that sort of thing!
A Z-Ring or Z-Power Ring is also required in order to perform Z-Moves. A Pokémon can only use a Z-Move if its Trainer is wearing a Z-Ring or Z-Power Ring and has the same Z-Crystal the Pokémon is holding. Mega Evolved and Primal Pokémon cannot use Z-Moves, even when holding an appropriate Z-Crystal (such as after Transform).

These Z-Moves are very powerful, but a Zenith Core can only fuel a single Z-Move per Scene. If an Interrupt is used so that the target is instead not hit by the move, the target instead takes damage as if 2 steps more resistant to the attack (just as Smite causes 1 more step of resistance for misses, these don’t stack, so using Protect against a miss is still only 2 steps more resistant on top of type matchups)

Note: If a Trainer is incapacitated before the Z-Move activation completely resolves, the Zenith Core’s charge is not expended and the Z-Move isn’t used, but the Trainer still uses their Full Action.

There are 18 different Z-Crystals that correspond to each of the 18 types, with several others that correspond to specific Pokémon. When a Trainer obtains a Z-Crystal that they can hold, they may then craft Z-Crystals that their Pokemon may hold. By default, a Trainer may only have the Zenith Core and one variety of Z-Crystal equipped at one time.

It is recommended for GMs to give a few Z-Crystals out to their players as valuable rewards for quests, prizes for winning tournaments, that sort of thing!
A Z-Ring or Z-Power Ring is also required in order to perform Z-Moves. A Pokémon can only use a Z-Move if its Trainer is wearing a Z-Ring or Z-Power Ring and has the same Z-Crystal the Pokémon is holding. Mega Evolved and Primal Pokémon cannot use Z-Moves, even when holding an appropriate Z-Crystal (such as after Transform).
